summary: Describes a mechanism for FTP clients and servers to implement security and authentication using TLS, with the FTP security extensions from RFC 2228. It covers the required subset and parameters. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Plain FTP sends files like postcards anyone can read. This memo puts the files in a sealed envelope using TLS.

subtitle: How FTP clients and servers upgrade to TLS using the AUTH, PBSZ, PROT and CCC commands.

tldr.problem: Plain FTP sends commands, passwords and files in the clear, and RFC 2228 defined security extensions without saying exactly how to use them with TLS.
tldr.mechanism: The client connects on the normal control port and sends AUTH TLS. After the TLS negotiation it sends PBSZ 0 and PROT to choose whether data connections are Clear or Private, and may use CCC to return the control connection to plaintext.
tldr.outcome: FTP gets authentication, integrity and confidentiality in an interoperable way, with the choice of protection left to client and server policy. It is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4217 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 4217 describes how three documents combine into a secure file transfer protocol: RFC 959 (FTP), RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 2228 (FTP Security Extensions). It is meant to give FTP TLS support in a way similar to SMTP in RFC 3207 and HTTP in RFC 2817.

TLS offers flexible security levels, strong server authentication, client authentication through TLS identities, and coexistence with the infrastructure already used for HTTPS. The RFC says SSL may actually be in use if the peers are configured that way; the session decides.

In summary, a session starts on the normal control port, the client requests TLS with AUTH, decides on data protection with PBSZ and PROT, and may later return the control connection to plaintext with CCC. Implementing this does not make every session secure; it provides the tools to negotiate an acceptable level.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP already had a way to ask for secret mode, and TLS is a good secret-keeping tool. This memo explains exactly how to plug the two together.

sections.title: Starting a Protected Session with AUTH
sections.content:
The server listens on the normal FTP control port (21), and session start is not secured. When the client wants protection it SHOULD send AUTH TLS. The server answers 234 if it will honour it. The 334 reply from RFC 2228 implies an ADAT exchange, which this document does not use, so it is incorrect here. The server SHOULD also accept TLS-C as a synonym for TLS.

A client that gets an AUTH rejection MAY continue unprotected. A server cannot dictate client behaviour in FTP, but it can refuse certain commands until the session is secured.

The client MUST still send USER even if the TLS negotiation supplies authentication, and the server decides which credentials to accept. After AUTH, transfer parameters (user identity, default data ports, TYPE, STRU, MODE and working directory) are reset, almost as if REIN had been issued.

If the server supports FEAT (RFC 2389), it MUST advertise AUTH, PBSZ and PROT, with TLS as a parameter of AUTH.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers first say hello in the open. Then one says, please switch to secret mode, the other says yes, and they start over politely by asking who you are again.

sections.title: Protecting Data Connections with PBSZ and PROT
sections.content:
The AUTH step secures the control connection only. To protect data connections, the client MUST send PBSZ and then PROT, and PBSZ must follow a successful TLS negotiation. For TLS the buffer size parameter is 0, because TLS looks like a streaming protection mechanism to FTP and the data is not encapsulated in buffers.

RFC 2228 defines four PROT values, but TLS needs only two: C (Clear, no TLS, so no authentication, confidentiality or integrity) and P (Private, TLS on the data connection). The initial state MUST be Clear. Once the server replies 200 to a PROT command, later data connections MUST use that level until another PROT is accepted, a REIN is issued, or AUTH is renegotiated. Clear may suit directory listings, pre-encrypted data or anonymous servers.

With Private, a TLS negotiation takes place on each data connection before any data flows. In all of the supported modes, the FTP client is always the TLS client and the FTP server the TLS server, whichever side opens the TCP connection. This holds for the classic PORT exchange and for the firewall-friendly PASV exchange. A server-to-server transfer is explicitly excluded, because neither server would be the TLS client.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the front door does not lock the delivery truck. For each parcel you choose: plain wrapping or locked box. Whichever computer opens the connection, the one who started the FTP chat is always the one asking for the lock.

sections.title: Clearing the Control Channel with CCC
sections.content:
Some sessions protect the control connection only during part of the session. The reason given is NAT and firewalls, which need to read the control connection to adjust their behaviour. Typically AUTH, USER, PASS, PBSZ and PROT are protected by TLS and then CCC returns the socket to plaintext.

The server replies 500 if it does not accept or understand CCC, 533 if the control connection is not protected with TLS, and 534 if it does not wish to clear the connection now. Otherwise it sends 200, shuts down the TLS session, leaves the socket open, expects the next command in plaintext, and accepts no more PBSZ or PROT commands. Later data transfers keep the current PROT setting.

The RFC says CCC has serious security issues and refers to RFC 2228. Clients should not assume the server will allow it, and servers may refuse it before the client has authenticated, to stop anonymous clients tying up resources with repeated AUTH TLS followed by CCC.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the door guard needs to read the notes you pass. So after the secret handshake you can switch the notes back to plain paper, while the parcels still stay locked. That is risky, so the server can say no.

sections.title: Policy and Failure Handling
sections.content:
A server may enforce policy: deny commands before TLS is negotiated, deny insecure or secure USER commands for certain users, limit TLS levels and CipherSuites, or accept TLS authentication in place of local authentication. For data, a server may forbid protection, let the client choose, insist on it, or decide per connection.

The server SHOULD check the PROT level only on the command that starts a transfer (STOR, RETR, NLST, LIST, STOU, APPE), not on PORT or PASV. Reply 521 says the data connection cannot be opened with this PROT setting. Reply 522, sent after 150 and after closing the data port, says the TLS negotiation failed or was unacceptable. A server may insist on a cached TLS session for data connections, which lets it avoid a full negotiation each time.

If TLS fails completely, the control connection is still unprotected and the server SHOULD send an unprotected 421 and end the session. If it fails during the handshake, the state is unknown and the connection SHOULD simply be dropped. Clients should be flexible about the timing of AUTH, PBSZ and PROT, since a server may require another command first.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is like a club doorman with a rulebook. If your lock is the wrong kind, he tells you with a number code, and if the handshake goes wrong in the middle, he just hangs up.

sections.title: REIN, ABOR and STAT
sections.content:
When the server processes REIN, the TLS sessions MUST be cleared and control and data connections revert to unprotected. Cached TLS sessions MAY be reused afterwards, but a server MUST NOT mandate this. If REIN is used to clear TLS, its reply MUST be sent in the protected session before the sessions are cleared.

FTP uses Telnet Interrupt Process and Data Mark with the TCP Urgent pointer to preface ABOR and STAT during a transfer. TLS does not support urgent data, so the server SHOULD NOT rely on SIGURG, and the client MUST send all data, including Telnet commands, across the TLS session.
sections.plainLanguage: If you press the reset button, the secret mode is switched off too. And the old trick of shouting for attention mid-transfer does not work through a sealed envelope, so you pass the message inside it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC assumes X.509 certificates. Server certificates should carry server identification much like those used for HTTP servers (RFC 2818). It is strongly recommended that the data connection use the same certificate as the control connection, or that there be another way to cross-check the identities. Without server certificates, for example with anonymous Diffie-Hellman, there is little protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. Client certificates are likewise an implementation decision, and without them a malicious client could still hijack a data connection.

Against the issues in RFC 2577: a bounce attack should be harder because the FTP server is always the TLS server and can drop data connections whose credentials differ from the control connection. Passwords and usernames are protected when TLS protects the control session. Port stealing is only prevented where strong client authentication is used. Privacy of logs and profiles is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock only helps if you check who is on the other side. So the data door should be opened by the same person who opened the front door, and the server can check that.

viz.caption: PROT LEVELS IN RFC 2228 AND WHICH ONES FTP WITH TLS USES

items.label: Clear
items.desc: Neither integrity nor privacy. Used with TLS: data connection made without TLS.

items.label: Safe
items.desc: Integrity without privacy. Not used with TLS.

items.label: Confidential
items.desc: Privacy without integrity. Not used with TLS.

items.label: Private
items.desc: Integrity and privacy. Used with TLS: TLS negotiated on the data connection.

items.label: AUTH TLS accepted
items.desc: The server will honour the AUTH TLS command.

items.label: CCC refused
items.desc: The control connection is not protected with TLS.

items.label: CCC declined
items.desc: The server does not want to clear the control connection now.

items.label: Wrong PROT setting
items.desc: The data connection cannot be opened with this PROT setting.

items.label: TLS on data failed
items.desc: The TLS negotiation failed or was unacceptable, for example a cached session was required.

items.label: Session ended
items.desc: Sent when the server ends a session after an unacceptable TLS negotiation.
